title: God's Field, God's Building, God's Temple
summary: Paul tells the Corinthians that their jealousy and quarreling show they are still acting like infants, not spiritual people. He and Apollos are only servants, one planting and one watering, while God gives the growth. The church is God's field and building, founded on Jesus Christ, and each builder's work will be tested by fire on the Day. The church is also God's holy temple, where his Spirit dwells, and anyone who destroys it will face God's judgment. Paul ends by telling them to stop boasting in human leaders, because all things belong to them and they belong to Christ.
story: Chapter 2 described the spiritual person, who receives God's wisdom through the Spirit. Chapter 3 turns that description into a mirror. The Corinthians think of themselves as spiritual, but their factions prove they are still worldly. Having shown what true wisdom is, Paul now shows what true leadership is, using three pictures: farming, building, and the temple. The chapter continues the argument about divisions that began in 1:10 and prepares for chapter 4, where Paul describes how apostles should be regarded and how the Corinthians have misjudged them.
historical:
Paul planted the church in Corinth around AD 50 to 51, and Apollos continued the work after Paul left (Acts 18:27-19:1). There is no sign that Paul and Apollos were rivals; in 16:12 Paul says he strongly urged Apollos to visit Corinth again. The rivalry was among the Corinthians themselves. Paul wrote from Ephesus a few years later, where he himself was building a church in a city dominated by a great temple, that of Artemis.

Corinth was full of building. After its refounding as a Roman colony in 44 BC, the city was rebuilt with temples, markets, colonnades, and public buildings, many paid for by wealthy citizens who were honored in inscriptions. The image of builders using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw would fit a city where fine buildings of marble and costly materials stood near houses of wood and thatch, and where fires could destroy whole districts.
cultural:
In the ancient world, agriculture and building were common pictures of teaching and community life. Paul says he laid the foundation "as an expert builder" (literally a wise master builder, architekton), the person who oversaw a whole construction project. The foundation, once laid, determined everything built on it. Builders in Greek and Roman cities were often paid and praised according to the quality of their work, and inspections could reveal shoddy workmanship.

The temple image carried great weight. Corinth had many temples, including those of Apollo, Aphrodite, and Asclepius, as well as shrines to the imperial family, and for Jews the temple in Jerusalem was the one place where God's presence dwelled among his people. The word Paul uses, naos, refers to the inner sanctuary, the dwelling of the deity, not the whole temple complex. To call a small, divided congregation of ordinary people God's sanctuary, with no building at all, was a startling claim. It also made division serious: to tear apart the church was to damage God's dwelling place.
literary: The chapter uses a series of images, each building on the last. Verses 1 to 4 use the picture of infants who can take only milk. Verses 5 to 9 describe a field, with planting, watering, and growth, and end with the summary "you are God’s field, God’s building". Verses 10 to 15 develop the building image, with a foundation, materials of varying quality, and a testing fire. Verses 16 and 17 shift to the temple, the most important building of all. Verses 18 to 23 return to the theme of wisdom and foolishness, quoting Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11, and end with a widening list (Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, the present, the future) and a final chain: all are yours, you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.

outline.t: Servants in God's field: planting, watering, growth
Building on the one foundation, tested by fire
Stop boasting in men: all things are yours

doctrines.note: The church is God's field, God's building, and God's temple. It belongs to God, not to its leaders, and its one foundation is Jesus Christ. Ministers are fellow workers in God's service, and the growth is his.

The Day will reveal the quality of each builder's work by fire. Some work will survive and receive reward, and some will be burned up, though the builder himself will be saved. Anyone who destroys God's temple will face his judgment.

God's Spirit dwells in the community of believers, making them his temple. Here the temple is the church as a whole (the "you" is plural); in 6:19 Paul applies the same image to the individual believer's body.

words.note: Naos, temple or sanctuary, the inner dwelling place of a god, distinct from the wider temple complex. Paul uses it three times in verses 16 and 17. The church together is the place where God's Spirit now lives. This is one of the New Testament's boldest claims about the church.

Themelios, foundation. Paul laid it by preaching Christ, and no other foundation can be laid. The word reminds readers that the church does not rest on the gifts or personalities of its leaders but on Jesus Christ himself.

Sarkikos, fleshly or worldly, describing behavior shaped by merely human ways of thinking. Paul uses it for the Corinthians, whose jealousy and strife show they are walking in the way of man. He distinguishes it from sarkinos in verse 1, which may mean made of flesh, simply immature; sarkikos suggests being ruled by the flesh.

Pur, fire. In the Bible fire often symbolizes God's presence and his testing judgment. Here it tests the quality of each builder's work on the Day: gold, silver, and precious stones survive, and wood, hay, and straw burn up.

christ: Jesus Christ is the one foundation of the church (verse 11). Every leader, teacher, and ministry must build on him and will be measured by him. The chapter also shows the order of belonging that runs through the universe: all things belong to believers, believers belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God (verses 22-23). That final phrase does not deny Christ's deity, which Paul confesses elsewhere, but reflects his role as the Son sent by the Father, a theme that returns in 11:3 and 15:28. The picture of the church as God's temple builds on Jesus' own words about the temple of his body (John 2:19-21) and on the New Testament conviction that God's presence, once located in the Jerusalem temple, now dwells among his people through the Spirit of Christ.

hard.q: Does 1 Corinthians 3:15 teach purgatory, or that believers can lose their salvation?
hard.a:
Verse 15 says that a builder whose work is burned up "will suffer loss" but "will be saved, but only as if through the flames". Different traditions have read this in different ways. The Roman Catholic tradition has cited this passage, along with other texts, in support of the doctrine of purgatory, a purification after death for those who die in God's grace but still need cleansing. Protestant traditions generally read it as a picture of the final judgment of believers' works, especially the work of teachers and leaders. On this view, the fire tests the work rather than punishing the person, and the loss is the loss of reward, not of salvation.

The context points primarily to church leaders, since Paul is speaking about those who build on the foundation he laid. But the principle applies more widely: God will evaluate the quality of what each person builds. The verse clearly teaches that a person can be saved while much of their work proves worthless, which is both a comfort and a warning. Verse 17 is a sterner statement: anyone who destroys God's temple, the church, will be destroyed. Interpreters differ on whether that warning applies to believers who harm the church or to outsiders who attack it.

questions: Paul says the growth comes from God, not from those who plant or water. How might that change the way you think about success or failure in ministry?
If your church is God's temple, where his Spirit dwells, what does that say about the seriousness of division and gossip?
Paul tells the Corinthians that all things are theirs. What would it mean to stop belonging to a party and start receiving every gift God gives through many people?
